utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Registrar -- Mr. Registrar, may I ask you to call the case on the Appeals Chamber's agenda.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-95-11-A, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now ask Mr. Martic if he can hear me and follow the proceedings in a language he understands. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I understand and I am able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now call for appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. Michelle Jarvis appearing today for the Prosecution together with my co-counsel, Mr. Paul Rogers; Ms. Laurel Baig; Ms. Kristina Carey; and Ms. Nicole Lewis; and our case manager today, Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence is represented by myself, lead counsel, Predrag Milovancevic; and my co-counsel, Mr. Nikola Perovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is the appeal hearing in the case of the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic. At the outset I will briefly summarize the background and substance of the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber as well as the manner we will proceed during the appeal hearing. The Appeals Chamber is seized of two appeals from the judgement rendered by Trial Chamber I in this case about one year ago, on 12th June 2007. The Trial Chamber found that Milan Martic participated in a joint criminal enterprise with several other individuals, the common purpose of which was the establishment of an ethnically Serb territory through the displacement of the non-Serb population. The Trial Chamber concluded that Martic incurred individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal for his participation in the crimes falling within the scope of the JCE. Martic was convicted of the following crimes: Count 1, persecution as crimes against humanity; Count 3, murder as a crime against humanity; Count 4, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; Count 5, imprisonment as a crime against humanity; Count 6, torture as a crime against humanity; Count 7, inhumane acts as a crime against humanity --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you please slow down a little bit for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- for the laws or customs of war. Count 9, cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war; Count 10, deportation as a crime against humanity; Count 11, forcible transfer as a crime against humanity; Count 12, wanton destruction of villages or devastation not justified by military necessity as a violation of the laws or customs of war; Count 13, destruction or wilful damage done to institutions dedicated to education or religion as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and Count 14, plunder of public or private property as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber acquitted Martic of Count 2, extermination as a crime against humanity. The Trial Chamber further found that Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb on 2 and 3 May 1995. It held that he incurred individual criminal responsibility pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute for ordering, under Count 1, persecutions as a crime against humanity; Count 15, murder as a crime against humanity; Count 16, murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; Count 17, inhumane acts as a crime against humanity; Count 18, cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war; and Count 19, attacks on civilians as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber did not enter convictions under Counts 16 and 18, having found that these crimes were impermissibly cumulative with Count 19. The Trial Chamber sentenced Milan Martic to a single sentence of 35 years of imprisonment. Now, let me come to the appeals. Milan Martic sets forth nine grounds of appeal against the trial judgement: An alleged error of law in not providing a reasoned judgement; alleged violations of his right to be tried by an impartial Tribunal and to be presumed innocent; an alleged error of law regarding the evaluation of evidence; alleged errors of law regarding JCE; alleged errors of fact in findings on JCE; an alleged error of law regarding the mode of commission of ordering; alleged error of fact in findings on the shelling of Zagreb; alleged errors of fact in making erroneous and insufficient findings; alleged errors of law regarding sentencing; and alleged errors of fact in findings on sentencing. Milan Martic seeks an acquittal on all charges. Alternatively, he requests that he be given a new trial or that his sentence be significantly reduced. The Prosecution sets forth one ground of appeal against the trial judgement. It argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law in finding that Article 5 of the Statute does not encompass crimes committed against persons hors de combat. It requests that the Appeals Chamber correct the legal error, revise the Trial Chamber's factual findings relating to counts charged under Article 5 of the Statute, and adjust Milan Martic's sentence accordingly. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo, and the appellants must not merely repeat the case they presented at trial. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. During the hearing, counsels may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation, but I would urge them not to repeat verbatim or to extensively summarize what is in their appeal briefs. I also wish to note that pursuant to the order for preparation of the appeal hearing of 29 May 2008, the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to address specific issues during this appeal hearing. I will not repeat here all the questions in that order. But in short, the Appeals Chamber specifically requested the parties to address the following issues. First, even if the Appeals Chamber were to find that hors de combat victims do not constitute civilians for the purposes of Article 5 of the Statute, should it nevertheless find that persons hors de combat are covered by that article? Second, the Appeals Chamber would like the parties to elaborate on what kind of link can be said to exist between Milan Martic and the various perpetrators "on the ground," in light of the factual findings made by the Trial Chamber. Third, the Appeals Chamber requested the parties to elaborate on the role of Milan Martic in the deportation and forcible transfer of non-Serbs as presented in the trial judgement. These invitations are made - I want to stress it - without prejudice to any matter that the parties or the Appeals Chamber may wish to raise. This invitation in no way constitutes an compression of an opinion on the merits of the appeals. Finally, I remind counsels that they may be interrupted at any time and invited to address specific questions posed to them by the Bench. The hearing will proceed in accordance with the Scheduling Order of 15 May 2008. This afternoon, counsel for Milan Martic will present his submissions for one hour and 30 minutes. Following a 30-minute pause, the Prosecution will present its response, after which counsel for Martic will reply. The hearing will then be adjourned and will continue tomorrow with the Prosecution's appeal. That having been said, I would now like to invite counsel for Martic to present submissions in support of his appeal. Please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In light of the schedule stipulated by the Appeals Chamber, I would like to just present very briefly key points regarding our grounds of appeal. In our brief we indicated some errors that the Trial Chamber committed, and I would like to start with one thing that might be very important for the position of the Trial Chamber. It is not merely an error of the Trial Chamber in the interpretation of Article 7(1) of the Statute regarding the joint criminal enterprise, but failure to distinguish between obligation of result and obligation of conduct. In paragraph 498 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber notes as follows: "The Trial Chamber" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to read slowly. It is impossible to interpret legal text at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, you should slow down. What is the page you mentioned, by the way -- the paragraph you mentioned. I didn't get it correctly, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is paragraph 498. Because of the tight schedule, I sometimes tend to speak faster, but I'll try to speak slower. So the Trial Chamber says as follows: "Martic held high positions within the SAO Krajina, including the Ministry of the Interior and president of the RSK. And because he held such -- holding such high positions he had absolute authority over the Ministry of the Interior." And let me quote what the Trial Chamber concluded: "Holding such positions, Martic was obligated to prevent the commission of crimes and to ensure that all inhabitants of the territories under his authority enjoyed respect for human rights." It appears, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber considered Martic to be an omnipotent god who was able to control every single individual and every single place in the territory of Krajina, whereas in essence there is a clear failure to distinguish between the obligation of conduct and obligation of result because Mr. Martic had the obligation of conduct, not of result. Well, this is quite clear from the position of the International Court of Justice in the Corfu case where the International Court of Justice clearly states that the mere fact that the state controls its own territory does not automatically mean that the state is aware of each unlawful act or of each perpetrator, nor was it supposed to know of each unlawful act or each perpetrator. In this case the Trial Chamber failed to understand that, so this is one of the reasons why it convicted Mr. Martic in this manner. Well, we've already noted that the Trial Chamber violated the right of the accused to be tried before an impartial Tribunal and the -- his right to presumption of innocence, and every accused has this right. This is quite clear from paragraphs 510 and 511 of the judgement, which in our view clearly show that the Trial Chamber was not acting as an impartial Tribunal and did not comply with the obligation to accord the presumption of innocence to the accused among other things because it -- because of the fact that he spoke unfavourably about the Tribunal and because of his conduct during the trial. The presumption of innocence is manifested, among other things, in the right of the accused to remain silent, not to present his -- not to testify in his own defence. This is indeed the right of the accused not to incur any negative consequences of his failure to defend himself or to -- his right to remain silent. Let me quote now from the Trial Chamber. "The Trial Chamber notes the Defence submission with the neuropsychiatrist's opinion describing Milan Martic as having a stable personality structure with a dominating quantum of emotions and finding him to be socially integrated, non-conflictive, and conciliatory - that's paragraph 511 - "but in light of Milan Martic's conduct demonstrated during the trial, especially the fact that he did not express any remorse for any of the crimes for which he has been found guilty, the Trial Chamber rejects this opinion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There is a problem. I'm not getting the English. Let's wait until they fix this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been improved. Everything's fine now. Thank you. So it is the position of the Defence that the presumption of innocence means that the conduct of the accused in the course of the trial may not in any way affect the issues of innocence or guilt of the accused or the assessment of his personality. The question of his personality is not only a factor which can be important in assessing the sentence should he be convicted, but it is also an important factor in establishing mens rea and establishing that there is the requisite responsibility. Such a violation of the right to the accused to be tried by impartial Tribunal and to be entitled to the presumption of innocence had devastating consequences to the decision taken by the Trial Chamber in items 1 and then 3 through 14 and 17 through 19 of this judgement. When it comes to the position of Mr. Martic in relation to this Tribunal, it is the position of the Defence that Mr. Martic had a negative attitude towards the selective approach taken to indictments. Many of those who were guilty of crimes against the Serbian population in numerous operations, such as Flash, Storm, and so on were not accused by this Tribunal. They remained living in Croatia, they received awards and commendations, and we believe that this -- there is not a single person who has a negative attitude to such a selective approach to accusing persons who are guilty. And this approach, in fact, was directed at the Prosecution and their attitude, their selective approach, in accusing certain people and not accusing others. Mr. Martic did not have a negative approach towards the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber failed to establish the main reasons due to which the Croats were leaving Krajina in 1991. This was, in fact, based on the request or instructions of Croatian authorities. The Trial Chamber failed to establish the fact that subsequent departures of Croatian population followed mass Croat attacks on UN protected zones where Serbian population suffered, and it is the refugees who created problems to the locals. In this particular case, the locals were of Croat ethnicity. Another error of the Trial Chamber - and I write "error" under quotation marks - is that the appellant's presumption of innocence was not abided by. This can be gleaned based on paragraph 342, where the Trial Chamber concluded that Milan Martic expressed a lack of interest for the fate of the Croat and other non-Serb population in persistent -- pursuance of the goal to create a Serb state, although in paragraphs 337 to 339 the Trial Chamber mentions a lot of pieces of evidence speaking to the contrary. In paragraph 341, they quote a whole series of evidence that speaks to the contrary. In our appellant's brief, we listed them individually, including the pages where they are mentioned; however, here I will only point out to Exhibit 966, which is a document admitted into evidence and it is referred to, it is quoted in paragraph 341 of the judgement. However, the Trial Chamber ignored this particular exhibit. This exhibit pertains to written statements signed by Milan Martic which was publicly published dated the 31st of December, 1991. I will quote the relevant part of the text: "Republic of Serbian Krajina and its Ministry of the Interior guarantees security to everybody living in these areas, and they call upon the citizens to protect people of other nationalities and their properties. There are no ethnically pure states anywhere in the world, and we believe that there are conditions needed for peaceful co-existence of everybody living in the Serbian Republic of Krajina, regardless of the general plan." This document was admitted into evidence, and it cannot be maintained that the Trial Chamber abided by the standard of beyond reasonable doubt when it ignored this particular piece of evidence. This total disregard of the presumption of innocence can be also gleaned from the way the Trial Chamber interpreted the ultimatum before the attack on Kijevo. It also completely ignored evidence concerning the Croatian policy towards Serbian population. It seems that the Trial Chamber ignored these facts because a member of the Trial Chamber was irritated when the conduct of his country was mentioned concerning international recognition of Croatia and its arming. This is the testimony of Witness Dobrijevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You are going too fast for the interpreters. Please slow down a bit, in reading especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will bear that in mind, and I apologise to the interpreters. Therefore, when Witness Dobrijevic at transcript page 10926 to 28 spoke about the fact that the events unfolded in the same way in 1991 as they did in 1941, the same sponsors of the war re-emerged in the new war. And it is an undisputable fact that Catholic church, Germany, Austria, and Italy were on the side of Croatia and that that was the reason why Croatia decided to get rid of the Serbs and commit genocide against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL REACTED BY SAYING
utterances.text: Perhaps because I am from Austria I feel a bit irritated by what you said about Austria, namely that it was one of the sponsors of World War II. So even a country which has a long-standing tradition of impartiality of Judges produced a Judge who felt he needed to stand up in defence of his country. However, the position of Judge Moloto was also significant. During the trial he believed that the issues concerning Croatian authorities and their attitude toward the Serbs were irrelevant, and he thought that it was irrelevant because Croatian authorities were opposed to Milan Martic, to Krajina, and to RSK. Milan Martic did not commit any crimes. Whatever he did represented attempt to fight against what had happened in World War II, the horrors of World War II, and their re-occurrence. The attitude of the Trial Chamber concerning the evaluation of evidence also shows numerous errors. The Trial Chamber, not in the main text of the judgement but rather in footnotes - namely footnotes 19 and 387 - showed their attitude. In footnote 19, the Trial Chamber said as follows: "The Trial Chamber interprets the standard beyond reasonable doubt to mean a high degree of probability; it doesn't mean certainty or proof beyond a shadow of a doubt." This is the explicit position of the Trial Chamber which is completely contrary to the jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice and to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, which should apply the highest possible standards, and in this case the Trial Chamber lowered the standard. The position in the Bosnian genocide case in the International Court of Justice was quite clear. That court required a very high standard of proof, high level of certainty appropriate to the seriousness of the allegations. So beyond reasonable doubt is nothing but a high level of certainty. This goes contrary to the position taken by the Trial Chamber, and this position is a well-established practice in all developed countries as well as in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. When it comes to the issues of the weight that needs to be attributed to certain evidence, that can be seen in footnote 387, where they evaluate the value of Milan Babic's statement and that of Witness M-003. In paragraph 34, concerning Milan Babic they said that this is a witness whose credibility has essentially been challenged and that needs to be supported by other evidence. And in relation to that, the Trial Chamber introduced a mathematical formula to evaluate the value of these two witnesses, and then they concluded that when it comes to a situation where one witness whose credibility was challenged supports the statement of the other witness whose credibility also has been challenged, that that alone is sufficient. We believe that this is unacceptable. Only credible and relevant evidence is of the essence when it supports evidence of any witness and supports it in such a way that it meets -- it leaves no room for any reasonable doubt. We have already mentioned that we believe that the way that the Kijevo ultimatum was interpreted was one of the indicators showing that it was not an impartial Trial Chamber that sentenced Mr. Martic. The Trial Chamber used this Kijevo ultimatum for coming to wrong conclusions about the existence of joint criminal enterprise, about its general purpose and goals. This is the most-often quoted piece of evidence in the evidence and in the entire judgement, and the most wrongly quoted piece of evidence. The text of the ultimatum is clear on its face. It can be found in annex on page 212, and in the text of the Kijevo ultimatum it says that this text was sent to the police administration Split, Kijevo, and to the local commune of Kijevo. The text of the ultimatum reads as follows, I'm quoting: "You and your leadership are responsible for the situation where Serbian and Croatian population can no longer live side by side in this territory any longer. This is why we will not allow your police units to enter any territory in this area because you continue Ustasha traditions in the so-called new young Croatian democracy." And then it says: "In the territory of Knin municipality in the village of Kijevo, there is your police station. By way of this ultimatum we are warning you that unless your police units withdraw within 48 hours from this village, we will attack with our forces your police station at the time that suits us. We also warned the population of Kijevo so that they can find shelter on time and thus not be injured. We reiterate that we wish the Serbs and the Croats to continue living in peaceful co-existence with fully guaranteed human rights to everybody. You will be responsible for any consequences that ensue as a result of failure to abide by this ultimatum." This is the verbatim text of this ultimatum, and there is not a single reason within this ultimatum to find that there existed a joint criminal enterprise and that Mr. Martic participated in that joint criminal enterprise. On the text of the Kijevo ultimatum, in the text it is clear that it wasn't its purpose to deport Croats from Kijevo or from any other village because they advised the population to find safe shelters on time. This speaks of the desire of Mr. Martic and authorities of Krajina to find a peaceful manner to co-exist for Croats and Serbs. That is why the -- Your Honours, again, I have problems with interpretation system. I hear the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This has been resolved now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try and continue. Perhaps this technical problem has been dealt with. Direct proof that the conclusions of the Trial Chamber about the contents of the Kijevo ultimatum are erroneous and as are conclusions about the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. We can find it in Exhibit 966. That's a document dated the 31st of December, 1991, signed by Martic in his capacity as the minister of interior where he says clearly that the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Ministry of the Interior guarantee security for everybody living in the area. They call on the citizens to protect citizens of different ethnic backgrounds and their property. An ethnically pure state does not exist anywhere in the world, and we believe that conditions are in place for the co-existence of all the people in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, regardless of the events in the broader context." Naturally, giving weight to the Kijevo ultimatum that it does not have, this is quite incomprehensible, this interpretation. The Trial Chamber goes on to make mistakes, and it errs when it says that the campaign of violence and intimidation or harassment of the Croatian population and the non-Serb population was a consequence of the position of the SAO Krajina and the RSK, that co-existence with Croats and other non-Serb citizens in the words of Milan Martic is impossible in that territory. The ultimatum is again completely misunderstood because it doesn't follow from it, and the ultimatum cannot -- the last two sentences quoted in paragraph 443 by the Trial Chamber where it says that the threat is clearly expressed in Milan Martic's ultimatum was implemented by creating an atmosphere of fear and the commission of crimes where the -- "it was impossible for Croats and non-Serb citizens to continue living there." The Kijevo ultimatum, Exhibit 966, and the whole pile of evidence says something complete -- says the opposite. The Trial Chamber made this error because it refused to take notice of some facts because it considered them irrelevant. Those facts were of a particular importance for considerations that relate to whether the JCE exists at all. These facts are of particular importance for the proper understanding of the Kijevo ultimatum, the -- for the proper understanding of the objectives of the Serbian leadership and their cooperation, and the question of who created the atmosphere of fear or corrosive atmosphere on the territory of present-day Croatia. When we're talking about facts of this nature, in the course of the trial the Trial Chamber publicly expressed its opinion that it considered them to be irrelevant. I think that it is a notorious fact that the Serb population lived in the territory of what is today Republic of Croatia for centuries as an ethnic community, as a people, and this territory corresponded to the territory of the SAO Krajina or the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In accordance with the Yugoslav Constitution and of Croatia's federal unit, they were a constituent people. The Trial Chamber decided not to take into consideration those facts, and it decided to ignore, to not take into account Exhibit 1019 that gave Serbs the right to self-determination that it had. At -- in testimony by Mr. Jarcevic at page 6186 of the transcript, he said that "because Serbs were a constituent people under the constitution, the Croatian government would not get the agreement of the Serb community to amend the constitution because it was required to get the consent of both nations," and that is why because Serbs knew -- the Croats knew that they could not get Serb lands out of Yugoslavia by peaceful means, that is why they started the war and why they started the persecution of Serbs in 1990. I'm quoting from Jarcevic's testimony at transcript page 6186. In paragraphs 84, 85, and 86 of our appellant's brief, we talked about the horrendous genocide committed in the territory of what is today Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia in World War II, while the independent state of Croatia was in place, where a million Serbs were massacred in the most horrendous way, in such a way that even German officers were appalled by what was going on. The Trial Chamber had in front of it all the evidence about that; it was on the record. And in our appeal we stated that Exhibit 941, that -- indicating that the German factory Solingen was requested by the Croatian authorities to produce a special kind of knife that would make it easier to slit the throats of Serbs. Well, the Trial Chamber set that aside. It set aside the fact that the president of the HDZ and the President of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, was a nationalist of the worst kind. Witness Macura said that at page 8193 of the transcript. The Trial Chamber likewise did not take into consideration the fact that up until the pre-election campaign launched by the HDZ in 1990, early 1990, the situation in Croatia was completely peaceful and inter-ethnic relations were good. Your Honours, all the Prosecution witnesses and all the Defence witnesses agreed on that. They all said the same thing: Situation was peaceful, inter-ethnic relations were good. After the HDZ won and President Tudjman was its leader, the process of secession from the rest of Yugoslavia began. Croatia seceded together with Slovenia; the inter-ethnic rifts began to be created; the single ethnic police force was created; and the harassment and persecution of Serbs began. There is a whole series of evidence about that. Witnesses Medakovic spoke about that at page 9164 and 9 -- or 8947. Witness Pupovac at page 10327. Prosecution witness Dzakula spoke about that at page 458 and 459 and many other witnesses. I don't want to waste your time here. Prosecution Witness MM-80 testified that the Croatian Democratic Union was arming illegally the Croatian population, providing them with automatic weapons, creating paramilitary units run by the HDZ. The Trial Chamber had all this information at its disposal. There was a plan for dissolution of the Serb question in Croatia, the removal of the prominent JNA officers and Serbs. I will speak about that at length later. Barriot, Witness Barriot, an UNPROFOR officer, testified at page 1074, said that it was obvious that everything that was done by the Croatian authorities was designed to terrorise Serbs. The very objective of the Croatian authorities was to kill or to expel the entire Serb population from Croatia, and this can be seen from what President Tudjman said in May 1996, and this is what Witness Macura said at page 8149 of the transcript, when the President Tudjman said: "The Serbian question in Croatia has been finally solved. There will never be more than 3 per cent of them." Yet, the Trial Chamber decided to set aside those facts, and we believe that this shows that it was not an impartial Tribunal. What errors we're talking about can be seen from Exhibit 237, that the Trial Chamber did not even mention. This is an intercept of a conversation between the defence minister and the interior minister, Mr. Spegelj and Bojkovac in October 1990 before conflicts broke out in the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Martin Spegelj in Exhibit 273 at page 4 is recorded as saying: "We will solve the Knin issue like that. We're going to slaughter them, and we will get international recognition for that. We will slaughter them." Now, the Americans are offering armoured vehicles and full equipment for 100.000 soldiers, all for free. Josip Bojkovac, minister of interior in Tudjman's Croatia, is recorded as saying in 273, Exhibit 273: "We will use any means at our disposal. We will use weapons, and Serbs in Croatia will never be what they used to be. Their supremacy is history. Their Knin will no longer be Knin. We will take over Knin. Knin is going to disappear. All Croats should bear this in mind, and we will establish a state no matter the price and no matter how much blood must be spilled." In this Exhibit, 237, Mr. Spegelj, defence minister of Croatia, says at the time when JNA was still in existence, that they would be killing JNA officers by shooting them in the stomach. But in order to understand the real intentions of the Croatian authorities towards the Serb population, and this is something that the Trial Chamber failed to take into consideration. This was not noted anywhere. It is very important what Martin Spegelj, Croatian defence minister, says in this exhibit, 237, at page 19. I quote: "If anything happens, issue an order to your people: Kill the extremists in the street, in the barracks, anywhere. Shoot them in the stomach. This will not be war. This will be civil war. There will be no mercy shown to anyone, women, children. Simply lob grenades into their apartments." There is a huge pile of evidence on record that was never even mentioned by the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, and this shows that these were not mere words, that this is what the objective was and this was implemented, and this is what President Tudjman says when he -- means when he says: "The Serb question in Croatia has finally been solved. There will never be more than 3 per cent of them." The Croatian policy of this kind enjoyed open support from Germany, the USA, Austria, Italy, the Vatican, Hungary, Slovenia. Exhibit 1015 speaks to that, Witness Jarcevic at page 6329 through 6330 of the transcript and a lot of other evidence. Witness Macura testified at page 8393 of the transcript that the delegation of the Republic of Serbian Krajina on the 3rd of August, 1995, in Geneva accepted all the proposals of the international mediator, Mr. Thorvald Stoltenberg, about the peaceful resolution of the Croat-Serb relations, but despite that it received information from the Russian mission in Geneva that the USA and Germany had green-lit the attack on Krajina by Croatia and that they would assist Croatia in that. The very next day, Operation Storm began. Operation Storm was the final stage of the implementation of the Croatian policy towards Serbs in Krajina. Let me quote what Spegelj, defence minister of Croatia said: "The Knin issue will be solved like this: We're going to slaughter them, and we will have international recognition for that." The Trial Chamber had all this in evidence yet disregarded it and failed to note it. Had it taken it into consideration, it might have gotten a more realistic picture about what the goals were of the Serb and Yugoslav leadership. The goals of the Serb and Yugoslav leadership were opposed to this kind of policy of the recurrence of genocide against the Serb population, and had it taken into account those facts that were on record, the Trial Chamber would have realized why Mr. Martic advocated an independent Serb state or at least a substantial degree of autonomy within Croatia because of such plans of the Croatian authorities which were finally implemented. The Trial Chamber not only ignored those facts but gave credence to what Mr. Babic, Milan Babic said, his uncorroborated evidence when he says in para 329 that Slobodan Milosevic covertly intended the creation of a Serb state and advocated those political objectives from the summer of 1990 until the end of 1991. Let me remind you - and this is what we explained in paragraphs 105, 106 of our appellant's brief - there is a huge pile of evidence showing that Slobodan Milosevic and Milan Babic did not actually agree. They were publicly -- they publicly clashed. An uncorroborated opinion of Milan Babic is not only an opinion by a person whose credibility has been impeached by the Trial Chamber itself, but we're talking about a person who in the middle of his cross-examination he put a plastic bag on his head and wrapped a belt around his neck and committed suicide. So he was obviously a highly mentally disturbed person who committed suicide in the middle of his testimony in front of this Tribunal, and the question is: How can his testimony be taken as credible evidence? Yet, the Trial Chamber accepts this testimony, opinion, by Witness Babic in paragraph 329, although they also had in front of them testimony by Charles Kirudja, a high-ranking UN official, a close associate of the special representative of the Secretary-General of the United Nations; Yasushi Akashi, an educated man, a man who was present as a representative of UNPROFOR in Yugoslavia for a long time who says that he attended meetings with Mr. Milosevic many times and that Mr. Milosevic never advocated the secession of Krajina from Croatia, that he was in favour of negotiations and in favour of autonomy for Krajina within Croatia, provided that the Serb ethnic community was protected. If the Trial Chamber had in front of it this evidence - and that's at pages 4898, 4899, and 4954 of the transcript - then this conclusion of the Trial Chamber about some covert objectives of Slobodan Milosevic, that's patently untrue and it cannot be considered to have been proven beyond reasonable doubt. And to conclude, there is not a shred of evidence which would support that the political goals or means for their realization were political goals -- or that political goals of Serbian or Yugoslav leadership amounted to forcible removal of Croats from Krajina. Let me reiterate that the JNA units had very clear orders to prevent any lack of discipline, any arbitrary conduct of any members, any departure from units, any improper attitude toward population of any ethnic background. That can be seen in Exhibit 59, but the Trial Chamber drew a conclusion that was completely contrary to that exhibit. In paragraphs 109 to 117 of our brief, we pointed out to the nature of the relationship among persons who are on the list that can be found in item 446 of the indictment where there is a list of members of joint criminal enterprise. What we pointed out to is that there is clear evidence showing that Milan Babic did not share the same objectives, motives, and intention with Milan Martic, Milosevic, Blagoje Adzic, Vasiljkovic, and other persons named in paragraph 446 of the indictment. Babic himself testified saying: "Even when I learned what had happened, I remained silent. I kept quiet. Milan Martic did what he could to fight crimes, and he called upon citizens to protect other citizens of other ethnic background and their property, saying that no ethnically pure state exists anywhere in the world and their conditions for peaceful co-existence of all ethnicities in this territory," Exhibit 966. This is why conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 453 to -- and 445 are completely wrong, complete contrary to the facts and evidence that was admitted; Trial Chamber ignored them. Trial Chamber also committed a particular error when in paragraph 449 they believed that Martic exercised absolute authority over the MUP. Martic, as minister of the interior, was a member of the government cabinet of SAO Krajina. SAO Krajina and RSK had its Assembly following elections. After the elections the Assembly appointed the cabinet, appointed ministers; Krajina had its laws which were in accordance with the Yugoslav laws and international law. Milan Martic carried out his functions as minister of the interior, fully in accordance with the law. There is not a single shred of evidence that Milan Martic, as a minister of the interior, ever ordered anything that was not permitted under the international criminal law or that he ordered something that could be used as a basis for indictment against him. I will remind the Chamber that the OTP brought here Mr. Ari Kerkkanen as their police expert who testified here on the 4th of May, 2006, and who in cross-examination when answering a question of the Defence said that he went over 100.000 pages of documents pertaining to the work of the police of Krajina and that out of that he selected 30.000 documents. And when counsel asked him whether he had found a single document showing that there was anything unlawful in the work of the police, he said no, such a document does not exist. There are documents that show something quite to the contrary, that everything was done in accordance with the law, that under difficult conditions existing in the war, Martic did everything in the power -- his power to protect everybody regardless of their ethnicity or religion. Possibly one of the reasons why the Trial Chamber misinterpreted wrongly Martic's authority and his powers, perhaps one of the reasons for that was the term Marticevci, meaning Martic's men. OTP witness Maksic, who an educated officer, colonel in the JNA who had completed very high military schools within the JNA who was there on the ground in 1991 and he was the OTP witness, he said on page 1191 of the transcript that he heard of the term "Marticevci," meaning Martic's men, that those were police forces of the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina and that this is how they were called. But it was a descriptive, perhaps even a derogatory term, Marticevci, meaning Martic's men, whereas those who sided with Babic were called Babicevci, meaning Babic's men. This was a colloquial term used in the streets when people would point to somebody and say, this person is a Babicevci, meaning Babic's men, or a Marticevci, meaning Martic's men. But in reality, that actually meant nothing. Whenever somebody here in this courtroom mentioned Martic's men or something similar, the Trial Chamber automatically and uncritically accepted as proven beyond reasonable doubt that those were members of the Ministry of the Interior headed by Milan Martic, even though in Exhibit 602 you can see that Milan Martic issued a written order, and in paragraph 4 it says that anybody who without authorisation wears police uniform or police insignia or has weapons of them or hold themselves out as police members have to turn themselves in to the competent military authorities and return weapons, police insignia, and so on. Anybody can abuse police insignia and police uniforms for their own purposes, and the Trial Chamber completely ignored this part of the evidence of Witness Maksic. When the Trial Chamber found that Martic was completely indifferent towards the crimes committed against the Croats, this can be seen in one of the paragraphs of the judgement, and it is unclear how the Trial Chamber came to this conclusion in view of Exhibits 908, 909, 906, and others. Under the leadership of Milan Martic as minister of the interior, the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK tried to prevent crime under difficult conditions. They worked under difficult conditions. First of all, let me point out to Exhibit 908, 908. This is the report of the clerk from the Knin district prison for 1994, and it is important for the following reasons. These are the exhibits that the Trial Chamber had available to them during the trial. On page 1, it says that in the district prison in Knin in 1994, a total of 151 persons were brought in. Against the above persons who were arrested, investigation was carried out due to reasonable grounds to believe that they had committed crimes. Further on in document 908, it says that the greatest number of these persons was investigated due to murder - 36 of them were investigated for them - 21, attempted murder; 19 were investigated for aggravated theft and so on. So the very fact that the perpetrators of the gravest crimes were in such high numbers arrested by investigative judges, this alone shows clearly that police prior to arresting them conducted on-site investigations. Then they found perpetrators, arrested them, and took them before investigative judge, who then signed an order placing them in the custody, that these people were then sent to the district prison, and then this report was produced. However, the Trial Chamber completely ignored this report. In Exhibit 909, which is the report of the Knin SUP sent to the Ministry of the Interior, which is to say that, yes, Mr. Martic was informed about the work of the MUP. He was very well informed, and he did everything in his power to combat crime. So in this document of the Knin SUP, it says this is the report about the gravest, most serious crimes which were committed in the territory of the Knin SUP. So in relation to 1992, there were 11 murders; 16 persons were killed, out of which five were Serbs and 11 were Croats. So out of 11, five were unresolved and six perpetrators were found in relation to six crimes. Five Serbs and one Croat were reported for crimes committed, and then there follows a list with the names of all perpetrators, all victims, with numbers of criminal reports that pertained to each of those perpetrators. In 1993, the report says that there were 12 murders in Knin; 13 persons were killed: One Slovene, three Croats, and nine Serbs. Four crimes remained unresolved, and then there follow names of victims, perpetrators, and the registration number of the criminal complaint. The same can be found in relation to 1994. This is clear evidence that police worked hard on uncovering perpetrators of gravest crimes, such as murder, grave bodily injury, and so on. And this tells us that it is hard to comprehend how the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that Martic was indifferent towards grave crimes that were committed and their perpetrators. It is very hard to understand how they reached their conclusion. I will show you the document that the Trial Chamber referred to and distorted its content. This is Exhibit 965, which speaks of the meeting between Mr. Martic and Cedric Thornberry, who was deputy of the UN -- commander of UN peace forces. The meeting was held on the 14th of June, 1993. This meeting was called at the request of Mr. Thornberry, and the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR members was discussed and also the issue of evacuation of people (Croats) who wished to leave the territory of Krajina. And the third item on the agenda was the peace process. On page 7 of this document, Mr. Martic in his discussions with Mr. Thornberry stated as follows: "As for the status of Croats in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we are doing utmost to protect them from violent people, and we have the same attitude, regardless of who is at risk, Serbs or Croats. We have identical attitude regardless of the ethnic background of people who are threatened." On page 3 of the minutes from this meeting, Mr. Martic when asked by Thornberry whether he had any complaints against the work of the civilian police says: "Sometimes they take it upon themselves to conduct an investigation on their own without us knowing about that, but we support the rule of law, and it is not our intention to conceal any crimes. You know that there are proceedings instituted against those who had committed crimes." Mr. Thornberry said, then, this: "Do you have any complaint about the work of the UN police?" And then Mr. Thornberry says to that: "I asked you that because our chief of police is answerable directly to me. I was told that he and you have very good cooperation and that your people respect our police." When Mr. Martic says to Mr. Thornberry that he has a problem with the Croats who wish to leave the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and then sign a statement saying that they're leaving voluntarily and then once they reach Croatian side they state that they had been deported and then Croatia uses that statement for their own propaganda and that this is why Mr. Martic wanted the UN to participate in that process so that the UN could confirm that these people really left of their own free will, and to this request of Mr. Martic, Mr. Thornberry said on page 8 of this exhibit, 965, Mr. Thornberry says as follows, and he was the deputy of the UN commander: "I think that this is exactly how it's done. We question everybody who wants to leave, and we can establish a procedure. I accept that you are protecting people under very difficult circumstances, and it would be good if you provided more information to the public about that." The Trial Chamber, however, completely ignored this document and, I think that the content of this document is quite unambiguous, namely, that Mr. Cedric Thornberry said, based on what his own chief of police told him, that Mr. Martic under very difficult war circumstances did everything in his power to protect the entire civilian population, regardless of their ethnicity; but the Trial Chamber came to a different conclusion. I also wish to point out that the issue was raised of detention units, the knowledge of Martic concerning that, and how the people in those detention units were treated and whether Martic was responsible for that. Your Honours, in the course of the trial the Defence brought here many relevant witnesses, educated persons, judges, people who served in police for many years, who held high positions in Krajina, Witness MM-90 who held a high post in the Ministry of Justice and in MUP and also in the government. He is a protected witness, so I can't give you any further details. MM-96, MM-116 and 117, all of them were protected witnesses. Witness Stevo Plejo, all of them confirmed that the prison system in the RSK was created by way of the decision of the government; that these prisons came under the Ministry of Justice and that they were within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice; that they had -- they employed their own guards; that the guards wore uniforms which were similar to police uniforms but they had nothing to do with police; that according to the law policemen were not allowed into the prison without the consent of investigative judge. Numerous witnesses confirmed this. Exhibit 906 is a document precisely from the district prison in Knin, and it is quite poignant because it shows what those prison units were. In Exhibit 906, we can see that the district prison in Knin sends a report to the Ministry of Justice concerning provision of information, and in nine pages they list the names of 40 persons employed as prison guards in the Knin prison. When it comes to personal particulars of that personnel, out of those 40 employees in 1994, 30 of them had high school education, two persons had junior college education, and two went to college. 27 employees worked in the Knin district prison from 1991. Out of those 27 who were employed in 1991, 21 were prison guards in the old Yugoslavia before the war. So these people had a long-standing experience of working in prisons in Croatia and in the old Yugoslavia. Out of 40 employees, as many as 30 worked as guards before the war. A high-ranking official of the justice ministry, Witness MM-90, spoke about that in detail, and he did say that the prison guards may have made some mistakes, but in -- they were then disciplined, and this is what Stevo Plejo said, that Red Cross missions came to visit and inspect the prisons every week and that it was impossible to hide anything from them. And the Trial Chamber just chose not to take that into account at all. In page 337 -- in paragraph 337, the Trial Chamber states that the information about the crimes were accessible to Mr. Martic as the minister of police in accordance with the rules of reporting that were in place. Then what is said in paragraph 337 shows clearly that the Trial Chamber fails to distinguish between the obligation of conduct and obligation of result. There is no police minister in peacetime conditions that is able to eradicate crime completely and to prevent any crimes from being committed, but it is a regular job of any police force, of Mr. Martic to identify perpetrators, to look for evidence, and to hand them over to the prosecutor's office with all the evidence, and the Trial Chamber had evidence in front of it showing that this was what was done. The deputy commander of the UN forces, Cedric Thornberry, confirmed that in the document that I have just quoted. I think you did take note of what he said: "I can see that you're protecting the Croatian population in very difficult conditions." Having said all that, Your Honours, and this was discussed in detail in our appeal, when you get to paragraph -- to the conclusion of the Trial Chamber at paragraphs 337 through 339, that there is no other evidence that measures were taken against the widespread criminal activities that occurred in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina between 1991 and 1995, then this conclusion is completely erroneous. This conclusion can only be drawn from a misrepresentation of facts. Even the exhibit that exists on the record, Mr. Martic's letter to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia where he is asking for help in order to fight crime, in particular serious crimes such as murder, where he asked for 20 to 30 inspectors to help him fight crime, the Trial Chamber interprets this gesture as participation in the JCE and not as Martic's efforts to get help for his employees to be able to put a stop to the evil things that are happening in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in the middle of war. I would like to stress that it is a position of the Defence that it is not the Defence's job to prove Mr. Martic's innocence; it is the Prosecution's job to prove his guilt and to do it beyond reasonable doubt. There is plenty of evidence in the judgement to corroborate what the Defence is saying: The conviction of Mr. Martic's Defence, that Mr. Martic did not commit any crimes, and that he promptly, appropriately, and lawfully performed his tasks, and that in the difficult wartime conditions the Trial Chamber completely set aside the fact that this -- all of this was happening in the war, that it has been proven beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Martic did not hate Croats, that he insisted in his public addresses that all citizens should be treated equally, urging the citizens to protect each other and each other's property, and that he was saying in public that there is no ethnically pure state anywhere in the world and that conditions were in place for a peaceful co-existence of all the peoples. The equality of citizens was shown in such a way, in such a non-discriminatory manner, that even the Serb refugees who fled from Croatia, who crossed into -- from the Croatian territory, they had to respect the law when they did so. This is what Witness MM-117 said at pages 9504 to 9505 of the transcript. French Colonel Bariott testified that in 1994 there were many Croats in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and that they enjoyed the same rights as Serbs; in other words, they were treated well. In Glina itself, there were hundreds of Croat families. There are reports of the international humanitarian organizations, Exhibit 1006, that confirms that. Witness Bariott, a medical officer, testified that he worked in the hospital in Glina where Croats worked, where patients were of all ethnic backgrounds and they were all treated the same; and as an example of this proper, humane treatment, he says that a Muslim woman underwent surgery, emergency surgery, and she had a haemorrhage. And what little blood there was, blood left in the blood supply in the hospital was used for her. So this is the humane, non-discriminatory treatment. Is this in line with how things allegedly were in this state led by Mr. Martic? Is this in line with what Mr. Barriot said at pages 10750 of the transcript? When Witness Medakovic spoke about the work of the police - he was the president of the Plaski municipality - he said that he asked Martic to give him weapons, to reinforce the police in a locale where there were only 20 police officers and 7.000 inhabitants, and they were unable to cope with the growing crime. And Martic said to him that weapons could be handed over only to those people who undergo training and who have proper authority and powers, that he didn't want to have any kind of vigilante police in Plaski. That's Witness Medakovic, page 8966 through 8967 of the transcript. Well, in light of everything that I said in my brief remarks at paragraph 342 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber errs when it says that the evidence showed that Milan Martic actively advocated and pursued the goal of creating an ethnically Serb state in spite of his awareness of the serious and widespread crimes which were being perpetrated against the Croat and other non-Serb civilian population. As a result of this policy, then it is quite clear that what I enumerated today, this position of the Trial Chamber is not something that has been proven beyond reasonable doubt. It is absurd. It is quite erroneous. A particular problem in the judgement delivered by the Trial Chamber is the treatment of the armed conflict in the spring and summer of 1991. The Trial Chamber erroneously finds in paragraph 443 that the armed conflicts that occurred in the spring and summer 1991 between SAO Krajina and the armed formations of Croatia were the result of the tensions between Croatia and Krajina police forces, and that the climate of fear and mistrust between the Croat and Serb population was something that was fomented. The Trial Chamber failed to find that the armed conflicts -- I only mentioned Exhibit 237 were the result of the policy pursued by the Croatian leadership towards the Serb population in Krajina, the Croatian leadership led by the HDZ, to create an independent state of Croatia that would not have more than 3 per cent of the Serb population. And let me remind you of paragraph 162 of the judgement, where it says quite clearly that the Yugoslav People's Army intervened in those conflicts to separate the two warring factions to prevent the further development of the inter-ethnic strife. Since we're talking about the conflicts in the spring and summer of 1991, when we're talking about Hrvatska Kostajnica, Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin - that's paragraphs 355, 354, 355, 359 through 363, 365, 174, 179, and others - it must be noted that the armed conflicts in Kostajnica cannot serve as a basis for the establishment of any kind of common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber itself quoted in footnote 418 that Kostajnica was liberated by the local population and that nobody -- no external forces participated in the fighting in Kostajnica, and that between 500 and 600 people participated in the fighting of Kostajnica on the side of the Territorial Defence. 117 were Croats, and there was a number of Muslims. So Serbs, 117 Croats, and some Muslims; the overall strength was 500 to 600. The Trial Chamber failed to find that in Dubica and Cerovljani there were National Guard Corps units set up there manned by people who were not locals. Josip Josipovic, Prosecution witness, spoke about that at page 3297 of the transcript; Witness MM-022 at page 2281 of the transcript. The Trial Chamber failed to take into account the fact that the commander of the National Guard Corps in Dubica and the commander -- or the president of the HDZ in Dubica was Tomislav Mateljak, and according to the testimony of Persecution Witness Josip Josipovic he was an unemployed scum who came into power and took part in arming Croats. So this was part of this drive to arm only one ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down when quoting numbers and pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's at page 3332 through 33 of Josip Josipovic. The ZNG, the National Guard Corps had its structures in Dubica, Bacin, and Cerovljani, and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, ordered the Croat forces to withdraw and the Croatian population to withdraw from that area. Witness Josipovic spoke about that at page 3308 and 3346. Witness Kozarcanin spoke about that, Exhibit 99 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 882 speaks about that, so the Croatian population left on the orders of the Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman. And witnesses confirmed that the population had left before the forces heading towards Kostajnica actually entered Kostajnica. Mr. Martic presented all that, and the Trial Chamber decided not to take this into account. Mr. Martic was convicted of horrible ordeals of the civilian population in Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin; and the Trial Chamber had in front of it almost absolutely reliable information that these crimes were committed by local renegades, people who were in conflict with any kind of authority, people who had nothing to do with Mr. Martic, and Witness Dobrijevic spoke about that at page 10889 -- 10888 of the transcript, and Witness Dobrijevic said, unfortunately, those people who wore all sorts of uniforms sometimes presented themselves as Martic's men, Martic's police or anyone else. They did all they could to gain authority, and they terrorised the population mostly at night in larger or smaller groups. They represented themselves as Martic's men, Dobrijevic says, and yet they never saw Martic himself at all. They had nothing to do with him, and they wanted to invoke the authority of the person who had the greatest authority in Krajina at the time. So they abused his name. That's what Witness Dobrijevic says at page 10889 and 10890 of the transcript. The Trial Chamber decided not to take into account the evidence of this witness. The Trial Chamber also had in front of it evidence to the fact that Mitrovic, the president of the Kostajnica municipality, was opposed to this renegade gang and that he sent regular police from Kostajnica to Dubica and that Radjunovic's men fired shots at this police force and in fact killed one of the police officers at the entrance to the village of Dubica. This is Prosecution Witness MM-022 at page 2316. There is evidence that a delegation from Banja went to Knin seeking help from Martic to prevent this negative development. In paragraph 338, the Trial Chamber found that Milan Bandic disbanded Radjunovic's police and replaced it by a military police unit that the local Chetniks were in conflict with Martic's men. But Exhibit 602 paints the real picture, wherein paragraph 1 of this order Martic explicitly orders that the police station in Kostajnica together with the military police before a police station is set up in the territory of Dubovica until it is set up that the police from Kostajnica should maintain public law and order in that area. That's an order from the 26th of November, 1991. The moment when Mr. Martic was informed by people from that area, he intervened. That was the first time he heard of that. He even asked for the intervention of the Yugoslav Army's members in order to return law and order to that area. Many witnesses confirmed this, and these same arguments can be applied to Bacin and Cerovljani. Innocent people were injured; they were injured outside of combat for no reason at all by outlaws who the Trial Chamber itself labelled as self-styled Chetniks opposed to Martic. And Martic was found guilty of their behaviour. When it comes to Saborsko and other locations, the Trial Chamber -- Lipovaca, Poljanak, and Vukovic, the Trial Chamber failed to establish a number of facts. First of all, Saborsko was a lawful military operation, Exhibit 108, the war diary of Tactical Group 2 which was admitted into evidence. This is the log-book from early November throughout the time when the JNA carried out this operation in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, may I advised you that you still have eight minutes for your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I keep track of time. In Exhibit 108, which is the log-book of the regular military formation of the JNA from early November 1991, detailing minutes, hours, and days during which there were permanent attacks of Croat illegal forces at the time because the JNA was the only legal military -- lawful military force at the time. So from Saborsko, Kuselj, and other villages they opened fire daily against the JNA barracks in Jesenica. When the Trial Chamber went on site visit, they were able to see that location and they were able to see for themselves that the JNA barracks in Licka Jesenica, which was constantly attacked by the Croat forces, can be seen clearly from Saborsko as though it was -- it was an open and unprotected target. The Trial Chamber ignored the witness Medakovic's statement on pages 8975 to 8977 of the transcript that from July 1990 Plasko with 7.000 inhabitants was completely surrounded - Plasko is the closest settlement to Saborsko - that the entire municipality was without electricity, telephone lines; it did not have a post office, did not have medical supplies, that the wounded were taken via forest roads to locations where they could be assisted, that the JNA units were under blockade. The Trial Chamber did not take into account testimony of this witness, Witness Medakovic, page 9030 of the transcript, that throughout the war in that city populated mostly by Serbs, Croats led a normal life. They had a Catholic church in Plasko which remained undamaged until the end of the war. The Trial Chamber also ignored the fact that the church in Saborsko, based on evidence presented during trial, was used as a machine-gun nest and as an observation post and that this was the reason it was damaged in subsequent operations. Exhibit 52 showed what the goals were of the attack on Saborsko; namely, the fire was opened against hostile forces, not against Croat population, unarmed population, and so on. No. The JNA units had clear orders to prevent any action against population. Based on evidence -- Exhibit 108, which is the log-book of Tactical Group 2, one can see that on the 7th of November when the crime in Lipovaca took place, the JNA barracks from early morning until the evening hours were constantly under attack. The Trial Chamber concluded that the JNA units walked around killing innocent victims, but the victims themselves from that area, for example, Marica Vukovic, said themselves that they didn't know who the perpetrators were. They were eye-witnesses, and they did not see them. Exhibit 107, we spoke about that in our appeals brief. There was a lawful military operation undertaken by the JNA against the Skabrnja Battalion. Both OTP and Defence witnesses confirmed that in Skabrnja there were about 730 people armed, that they used automatic weapons, they had helmets, flak jackets, and they had minefields, and they attacked the JNA airport which was located in the vicinity. Nobody wanted to attack innocent civilians. They wanted to attack the perpetrators of the crime, and those perpetrators should be found and punished, not Mr. Martic. I only have three minutes remaining, and I wish to say that the witnesses from Bruska, Jasna Denona, the survivors from Bruska and Ante Marinovic, and also the girl Denona who was operated on twice in the Knin hospital and her life was saved there; Ante Markovic's life was also saved in the Knin hospital. He as a Croat was gravely injured, and by his own testimony he spent more than one year in a nearby Serbian village, which was completely armed, but not a hair on his head was hurt. So what kind of a terrible situation Martic himself and his people created if Croats lived without any injury protected by the Serbian neighbours. Perhaps the Trial Chamber came to this erroneous conclusion as a result of a prejudicial statement of Judge Moloto, who during the testimony of Lazar Macura said as follows: Why did you Serbs not move out of Croatia given that Croats don't like you, or if Croats don't like you? That question posed by Judge Moloto is identical to the question put to Jews that would say, why did you Jews not move out of Germany if you saw that Hitler was placing you in concentration camps? The Trial Chamber showed identical attitude of concealing Croat crimes when they spoke about the attack on Zagreb in paragraph 468. The Trial Chamber when analysing whether those were lawful actions or not says: "Even if the Trial Chamber were to suppose that the Croat forces engaged in serious violations of international humanitarian law during Operation Flash," this is something stated by the Trial Chamber which had in front of it numerous pieces of evidence pointing to the contrary. They have Exhibit 112, which says that in the village of Baklenica [phoen], item 1, reports on the 1st of May: Massacre, five wounded, and three nurses were killed, slaughtered, their necks slashed. In item 4, it says at the intersection between villages Trnakovac and Gropoje [phoen] some people were ambushed. Machine-gun and sniper fire was opened against them, and there were 50 victims. In item 5 in this UN report, it says in the village of Vares civilian population, including women and children, travelling on foot and in cars were subjected to fire. Hundred people were killed, and they list names of individual victims. And these are only the cases where the names of victims were known, and the Trial Chamber in this paragraph says if we were to suppose that the international humanitarian law was violated, this is wilful concealment of Croat crimes; this is what it amounts to. The Trial Chamber had evidence before it that by way of Operation Flash Croatia violated the cease-fire from 1994. It violated the UN mandate. It violated the essence of the UN charter saying that all hostilities need to be resolved by a peaceful means. Despite of that, Croatia drastically violated international humanitarian law by expelling 20.000 Serbs. There are numerous evidence supporting this, and one has to wonder how the Trial Chamber could have reached this conclusion and this judgement. Perhaps the response can be found in Exhibit 237 where Croatian general in October or November 1990 says: "We will resolve the issue of Knin by slaughtering them, and we will gain international recognition for that." Now, I wonder whether the Trial Chamber concealed this fact by handing down this kind of judgement. Thank you. I've concluded.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and thank you, my learned colleague, but it's already been done. utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm grateful.
