utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I will be dealing with ground 5 in this response, and my learned colleague, Ms. Baig, will address question 3 to Your Honours' questions. And if there is time and Your Honours so wish, Ms. Carey is available for questions relating to the Zagreb shelling counts, but it may be that we don't reach that stage in proceedings. Your Honours, during the course of my submissions I will also be dealing with Your Honours' question 2. Your Honours, the defence challenge the conviction in this matter, really, on two premises, first of all, that there is no criminal purpose, and an add-on to that is that the purpose was legitimate, political objectives, or legitimate self-defence, and that arises out of the reply brief at paragraph 59 and his appeal brief at 105 and 106. He also develops his submissions by saying if there was criminal activity then he was not a party to it. That's at his reply brief 41, but he implicitly and actually accepts that there was criminal activity going on during the period. That's in his appeal brief at 57 and his reply brief at 40. And essentially, and Your Honours will forgive me for reframing your question 2 slightly, the last point, his involvement, is the subject of question 2 to the extent: What is his connection between himself and the principal perpetrators, having regard to the Appeals Chamber judgement in Brdjanin. Your Honours, in developing this response, can I deal with it this way: First of all, our primary response to these challenges is of course that the Trial Chamber correctly identified all of the legal elements set out in Brdjanin at paragraphs 429 and 430, and to touch them. First of all, they established his intent at 453, that he participated together with the other JCE members in a shared criminal purpose and that he had the requisite mens rea for the JCE 3 crimes. That's at 454 of the judgement. They identified the plurality of persons that shared the common criminal purpose at 446, and they identified the fact that the purpose resulted in the intended crimes at 480. And finally, that his contribution - and I suspect that is where Your Honours are most focused - amounted to a significant contribution to the crimes forming part of the common criminal purpose, and it's worth reminding ourselves that the common criminal purpose crimes were deportation and forcible transfer. That's found 447 to 454 of the judgement. The other crimes were the JCE 3 crimes, and that may be significant. In developing this response, I will address Your Honours on the common control purpose briefly, who the members were and what their role was, and finally his responsibility for the crimes of the principal perpetrators, either directly or through another JCE member. And in so doing, I hope to have answered Your Honours' question 2. Your Honours I hope will forgive me for dealing with it in this way rather than going directly to question 2 because I hope to set up the framework in which I will respond to Your Honours' question 2 in this way. What was, then, the criminal purpose? Obviously, it was criminal from the outset in our submission. Having heard the evidence over many months, the Trial Chamber found this to be, 445 in the judgement: " ... the establishment of an ethnically Serb territory through the displacement of the Croat and other non-Serb population as charged in Counts 10 and 11." So that refers it to the methods of the crimes that we're concerned with that I have already identified, and Your Honours of course have touched that in the opening address this afternoon. In their words: "From at least August 1991, the political objective to unite Serb areas in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia in order to establish a unified territory was implemented through widespread and systematic armed attacks on predominantly Croat and other non-Serb areas and through the commission of acts of violence and intimidation," judgement 445. They went on: "This campaign of violence and intimidation against the Croat and other non-Serb population was a consequence of the position taken by the SAO Krajina and subsequently the RSK leadership that co-existence with the Croat and other non-Serb population in Milan Martic's words, 'in our Serbian territories of the SAO Krajina' was impossible." The scope of the enterprise was addressed at 443 of the judgement when they said: "The evidence shows that beginning with the armed attack on the predominantly Croat village of Kijevo in August 1991, the SAO Krajina MUP and TO forces cooperated with the JNA. As of this point in time," I remind Your Honours August 1991, "the JNA was firmly involved on the side of the SAO Krajina authorities in the struggle to take control of territory in order to unite the predominantly Serb areas." They found: " ... these attacks followed a generally similar pattern, which involved the killing and removal of the Croat population." And that those attacks were -- the primary objective of those attacks were the crimes that were outlined as part of the criminal purpose. So to move from the purpose now to who the members were and what their role was, and, Your Honours, the significance of course of this is to identify how ultimately the principal perpetrators are identified with a member of the JCE. The Trial Chamber prefaced its remarks on finding who the members of the JCE were by stating, and this is significant with respect: " ... the cooperation between the armed forces of the SAO Krajina, and later the RSK, and the JNA, was extensive and covered such major military actions as those carried out in Kijevo, Hrvatska Kostajnica, Saborsko, and Skabrnja ... the evidence of Milan Martic's arrest in 1991 gives a clear example of joint cooperation between political leaders in the SAO Krajina, in the RS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in Serbia," judgement 446. Following on from those findings, the Trial Chamber identified the members of the joint criminal enterprise. Those members were the political and military leaders of the SAOK and the SFRY, and of course to some extent Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. If I can put it this way, representing the JNA in those findings were Blagoje Adzic, general; Veljko Kadijevic, general; and SFRY federal secretary for defence, trial judgement 330; Ratko Mladic, JNA general and commander of the 9th Corps known as the Knin Corps. The political representatives were Slobodan Milosevic; Radovan Karadzic; Franko, Frenki, Simatovic; and Jovica Stanisic. The SAO leaders were represented by Milan Babic, SAO Krajina president and commander of the territorial forces, the TO; and of course the accused, Milan Martic, both political leader in the SAOK structures, as minister of the interior, ultimately of course as president, but also as a commander, a commander of those ministry forces of the MUP and the SAOK milicija, a word identified with the police. And he was for a period the TO deputy commander. There is another, also, part of the SAOK, Captain Dragan Vasiljkovic. Perhaps he's the only one that comes out of the political military leadership and goes down to a more, perhaps, pragmatic, practical level as a trainer of forces. Your Honours, their role as political and military leaders of armed groups in furthering the common criminal purpose has been demonstrated by the regular cooperation between those members, both militarily and politically, as set out in the judgement at 140 to 143, 159, 446, and 448. In addition, the Chamber found at paragraph 330 that the JNA deployment was, according to Kadijevic, a member of the JCE, based on "full coordination with Serb insurgents in the Serbian Krajina." This proves, we say, that these groups were not acting alone but were acting together through coordination and cooperation. And this leads on to consider with whom the JNA coordinated their actions. The Trial Chamber found that the armed forces of the SAO Krajina cooperated with the JNA, 446 and 142. That of course begs the question: Who were the armed forces? The armed forces, the Chamber found, from the 1st of August, 1991, of the SAO Krajina were the Milicija Krajine together with the TO. That's 137. The TO, of course, Territorial Defence organizations, but perhaps the significance of this organization was that it was and was described and found by the Trial Chamber as wearing solid colour JNA uniforms with the words SAO Krajina in Cyrillic on the sleeve. Who were the Milicija Krajine? They were within the MUP, trial judgement 135. At Exhibit 498 within the record, an interview given by Milan Martic on the 7th of July, 1991, with Politika, and referred to in the judgement in other ways at footnotes 293 and 1038, is significant because in this interview he describes himself who the forces were. And as minister of the interior, one might expect him to know who was within his command. They were, he said: "The Krajina police has its regular forces, which perform the duties related to internal affairs, its reserve forces, and the SAO Krajina special units." And in the same interview he referred to these forces as "my fighters." "My fighters." In considering how the units act together, the Chamber found that resubordination of the MUP units to the JNA required prior approval by the minister of the interior, of course Milan Martic throughout, trial judgement 142. It was either fully under the control of the JNA or it was under control of the commander of the individual MUP unit, those of course all coming within the ministry, depending on whether it was cooperating or was resubordinated formally, judgement 142. General Adzic required that all armed units "be they JNA, TO, or volunteer units, must act under the single command of the JNA," 12th of October, 1991, Exhibit 26, referred to in judgement 142, footnote 297. And they found there that: " ... after the beginning of summer 1991, the SAO Krajina TO was subordinate to the JNA." The statement that volunteer units acted under the command of the JNA is also borne out by the evidence of Colonel Maksic, who my learned friend referred to, the colonel from Belgrade who was -- and that's not insignificant, that in September of 1991 he was sent from Serbia, Belgrade, to help set up the staff of the TO at the request of Babic. He was sent from Belgrade to do that. He said: "At the time," and he was there from September 1991 through to December 1991, and you'll recall my learned friend explaining what I think was aimed at his credibility said this: "At the time," he said, to my knowledge, there were not any paramilitary formations that were independent and active in the area. There was one unit belonging to the Serbian Radical Party, but it was in the structure of the 9th Corps. It was part of its organic structure and was not in any way different from the other units that were part of the 9th Corps." That's transcript reference 1194. Your Honours would have heard reference to the local Serbs, but in our submission when used by the witnesses this is most often used in describing people they knew or who were local to the region, but invariably we submit these local Serbs were acting as part of or in cooperation with an armed group, such as the TO, the JNA, and the Milicija Krajine. See, for example, Witness MM-022 in the judgement at -- sorry, transcript reference T2343 to 4. This witness is quoted extensively throughout the judgement. What, then, was Milan Martic's role? He acted, we say, in cooperation with the other members of the JCE, and the Trial Chamber found that at 448, 446, 140 to 143, and 159. He does not dispute Serbia's assistance in arming the milicija, in financing the government of the SAOK - that's his appeal brief 109 - nor that he cooperated even closely in joint military operations - reply brief 62 - or with the Serbian MUP and the SDB, reply brief 63. He even asserts in his appeal brief at 108: " ... help from Serbia was not a secret, but that help did not include support to Babic but to appellant." [Sic] He set up the Golubic camps, judgement 144. These camps were for training forces that were at that time the only -- according to Maksic the only armed force in the Krajina. Those activities included at the training artillery training, mining training, sniper shooting, trial judgement 145. They found the training was primarily military in nature. Bearing in mind, these units at that time were part of the police. They didn't appear to be trained to issue tickets but were given military training. Medakovic was a Defence witness, commander of the Plaski milicija unit having been through the training at Golubic, a witness already referred to by my learned friend, and described having been taught how to carry out mopping-up operations as part of the training, T8971. These training camps, Your Honours, were set up before the main series of attacks began in July and August of 1991. This training was ongoing and of course raises the question as to why it was happening if there were peaceful intent. The TO and the police were also used in mopping-up operations. In our submission, this is a phrase with a sinister connotation. Exhibit 133, the 4th of October, 1991, an order to the TO Glina said: "When mopping up the terrain, spare Pajo Bubas and his wife, who is a Serb, and their home. They have been verified as loyal people ..." Babic at transcript 1573 provides further evidence about this cooperation, and he says this: "The police forces," at line 23, "the police forces or the parallel structures as we called them would stage provocations. JNA units would move in with artillery and launch an attack and advance. They would be followed by TO milicijas, volunteer units who would loot and torch. "Judge Moloto: And torch what? "The Witness: "Croatian houses." Your Honours, clearly from the outset the military cooperation was seen in an organized way and the role of the TO and the police units was in this -- if it wasn't directly in the attack, it was certainly in this mopping-up. And Your Honours will recall that many of the crimes that are the subject of this indictment were -- arose in the immediate aftermath of the attacks in the mopping-up stage, some of them of course during the attacks but many of them in that latter stage. There was further evidence that Martic was in control himself of units and provided units involved in those attacks and was involved in the planning and preparation of attacks. They found he participated at 163 in the attack on Lovinac with a fellow JCE member Simatovic. Mladic is reported as stating in the minutes of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly of Serbian People in May 1992, Exhibit 45 at page 48, which is, when Your Honours look at it, much more of a verbatim record than what we might understand as a minute. It is a -- almost as though the entire speech has been written out. It's quite a lengthy document. But in there, he said -- Mladic said this: "The Knin Corps was successful because under a single command in the zone of the corps were the JNA, the Territorial Defence forces, and Martic's police. Isn't that right, Martic?" Martic, obviously being there. "And because he and I, I call him and say, Give me 40 policemen here at Kijevo, and you took part in the fighting. Isn't that right, Milan, and we did what we had planned ..." What they did is found within the trial judgement relating to the village of Kijevo. In Kostajnica, he coordinated combat activities together with JNA Colonel Smiljanic. He ordered a cease-fire directly on the 5th or 6th of August, 1991, in the report of the 6th of August, Exhibit 38, which was directed to the TO units of the SAO Krajina, footnote 599. He ordered arms for the TO, Exhibit 41, footnote 292, trial judgement 141. He attended briefings of the JNA 9th Corps, evidence of Maksic, T1168. He issued orders to units being used in mopping-up operations in Lovinac, 17th of September, 1991, Exhibit 40; footnote 679 is an explicit reference. He had to be asked to provide units to be used by the JNA, Maksic, trial judgement 142; he attended planning meetings and received copies of orders relating to those units, Maksic, 1166. He exerted control over the police unit in Hrvatska Kostajnica in November/December 1991 when he disbanded it, trial judgement 338. How, then, were the principal perpetrators linked to Milan Martic or another member of the joint criminal enterprise? Your Honours, our submission is this: The crimes that occurred were as a result of the use by the JCE members of the JNA, TO, Milicija Krajine, SAO Krajina armed forces, paramilitaries, and other local Serbs to achieve their criminal aim. Use is in the context of the common purpose, so the use is to further the criminal purpose with the mens rea of that criminal purpose with a high level of shared intent. That is the way these members cooperated together is implicit from the judgement. The emphasis placed on cooperation between the forces throughout the judgement, particularly 443, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 9 - that's 445, 6, 7, 8, and 9 - the finding about Martic's involvement in the forcible transfer and deportation of the population through his own acts and acts of the MUP, trial judgement 452, which refers back to the totality of the acts in sections 3D 2 to 5 of the judgement, and the reminder that the primary purpose of the attacks was to displace the population. Your Honours, what do I mean by use? The assessment of use in our submission is a purely factual assessment on a case-by-case basis, words which I'm sure are familiar to Your Honours from Brdjanin's Appeals Chamber judgement 413. This can be inferred, as Your Honours held, from various circumstances, including the fact the accused or any other member closely cooperated with the principal perpetrators in order to further the common criminal purposes, Your Honours' judgement at 410 in Brdjanin. It could be use in the sense of ordering or a less-rigid structure, or it could be use through a hierarchy. Those are ways in which evidentially use could be established. We accept there does need to be a link between the principal perpetrator and one member of the JCE, but this need not but on the facts may be Martic himself. To answer how the link arises, we must identify the principal perpetrators. Your Honours, I've already identified the leaders of those groups of perpetrators, and I've demonstrated, I hope, how the groups -- how the Chamber found the groups were working together to implement the common criminal purpose. For the majority, the Trial Chamber found that the principal perpetrators were Milicija Krajine, JNA, TO, SAO Krajina forces, or some combination of these. So they clearly linked the perpetrators to the groups, and we know who controlled the groups and how they were used within the purpose. In addition, there were references to other soldiers or paramilitaries, but this in our submission is always in the context of operations where they were acting in cooperation or were subordinated to other units of the JNA or the TO. In addition, there is clear evidence that the JNA tightly controlled the zones of operation, for example, Exhibits 607, 53, and 57. The Trial Chamber did not find any of the principal perpetrators to be actual members of the JCE. So to go through some of the crime sites: Hrvatska Dubica, the Trial Chamber found the Milicija Krajine were responsible for the killings that occurred and for the plunder that occurred in that region, the Milicija Krajine, the JNA, the TO. In Cerovljani, they found that murders were committed by the Milicija Krajine, JNA, or TO, or a combination. The destruction in Cerovljani they found was committed by armed Serbs. But, Your Honours, that must be taken in the context of the military operations that were being carried out in that area; and in the judgement at trial judgement 175, 179, and 180, the Chamber deals with the operations that were being carried out in that area throughout the period in September of 1991. And the significance is that the crimes of destruction took place on the 13th, 21st, and 24th of September, 1991; and we can see, for example, at trial judgement 179 that on the 15th of September, 1991, the JNA, the TO, and the police surrounded Predore, approximately 8 kilometres from Hrvatska Dubica. If I could ask Your Honours to look with me, please, in Sanction at map 11. I hope just to show quickly what the physical location of these villages was because it helps to understand or may help Your Honours to understand the extent to which these operations were being carried out. The first map just shows you the region of Kostajnica, and then the second image shows the villages highlighted to the right-hand side. I'm sorry it's a bit small. If we blow up the next one, the writing suffers slightly, but I think it's probably easier to see. Predore, the judgement found there were operations between the JNA, TO, and police around that village on the 15th of September, 1991. You can see Cerovljani just below and Dubica just below that, and Bacin which are crime sites, Your Honours will recall. The scale on this map is about 8 kilometres from Predore to Dubica. Of course, from Predore to Cerovljani is a smaller distance. The significance being that the Chamber found also that Dubica was taken over on the 15th -- 14th or 15th of September, Your Honours, forgive me, but it was the 14th or 15th of September when Dubica was taken over, and a headquarters for the TO -- at least local headquarters of the TO and Serb forces was established in Dubica at that time. It's only a few kilometres from Cerovljani. So it was a reasonable inference, in our submission, that the Chamber made the findings that it did. Bacin also found that the Milicija Krajine, JNA, TO, or a combination were responsible. Saborsko was a planned attack; there's no doubt about that. The -- those responsible for the crimes were found to be members of units present in Saborsko, at judgement 379. Those members were identified at 225 as being Tactical Group 2 within the JNA 13th Corps, including the Plaski SDB, Plaski TO, and the Milicija Krajine. Medakovic was the commander at that time of the TO and had previously been commander of a unit of the Milicija Krajine. And he said that after the attack there were many Serb soldiers and policemen in the centre of Saborsko. Destruction was similarly held responsible by those parties to the forces that were involved in the attack, as was the plunder. Skabrnja was also a planned attack. The principal perpetrators there identified variously one -- is referred to as a local paramilitary soldier wearing a camouflage uniform with an SAO Krajina patch, but critically this: Who participated together with other SAO Krajina forces in the attack on Skabrnja, 386. Three others were killed by other members of such paramilitary soldiers. How those units were made up is found at 244 to 7. There's a reference, also, to Chetniks, paramilitary soldiers, but clearly in the context of them working together with the forces. The Pavicic house, again, SAO Krajina forces in the attack on Skabrnja, Grgica Segaric similarly, and I could go on, but those are the broad findings for those groups. And then for killings that appear to have occurred in the immediate aftermath, because the Chamber list two other groups where they can't quite identify the time, it appears, as to when the victims were killed between the 18th of November, 1991, and the 11th of March, 1992; the trial judgement finding is at 392. They set out that these victims they were satisfied were killed by members of the units including JNA and TO which took part in the attack on Skabrnja or which were subsequently present in the area of Skabrnja following the attack, and these included JNA units, units from a TO brigade under JNA command, and paramilitary units. Skabrnja, 11th of March whereby 1992, is the next group of findings, which is a small group of victims, and they found that JNA soldiers had been present in the village in December and that subsequently there was a TO brigade under the JNA in the village, were reducing numbers of JNA soldiers, but replaced by soldiers with SAO Krajina patches on their camouflage uniforms guarding and patrolling the village. They found that the killings were perpetrated by those -- one or more of those groups. Your Honours, I'm not going to go through each and every other one of the crime sites. I could, but it may not be helpful because the findings where they are listed are within the judgement, of course. I think the principle that I've tried to establish is that the labels that have been applied are clearly identified and that those groups have been identified as acting together during the course of this criminal enterprise as part of the planned purpose. They themselves, of course, may not have known precisely what the purpose was, but the organization was at the higher level. Your Honours, the Appeals Chamber, to summarize, in Brdjanin at 409 considered that the Appeals Chamber decision in Stakic was a precedent not to be lightly dismissed. This case is similar to that of Stakic in that the members of the joint criminal enterprise were all political and military leaders, save for Captain Dragan. The common purpose was clearly carried out by a larger number of individuals who were instrumentalised by their heads, who were JCE members, including in this case TO, JNA, the police, and paramilitary forces. The principal perpetrators were being used by a member of the JCE to fulfil the common purpose to displace the non-Serb population. There is no finding that they were members themselves, so they were either willing tools or they were innocent agents, but for this argument, in our submission, it matters not. The cooperation between the JCE members and the widespread nature of the crimes reveals the extensive use of the various groups of perpetrators to achieve the common criminal purpose. Indeed, the cooperation between the tool groups show the extent to which their actions were coordinated by members of the JCE at the highest possible level. The assessment of use as I've already submitted is a factual assessment on a case-by-case basis. I don't apologise for repeating the words of this Chamber in Brdjanin at 413. It can be inferred from the various circumstances, including the fact that the accused or any other member of the JCE closely cooperated with the principal perpetrator in order to further the common criminal purpose. Your Honours' decision in the Brdjanin appeals judgement at 410. Whilst committing the crime or crimes, they also committed the other foreseeable other crimes, the JCE 3 crimes. Martic's contribution to the common purpose I have already outlined. His contributions were not minimal. The crimes were committed. Your Honours, we submit the principal perpetrators were tools in the hand of one or more JCE members as they fulfilled their part of the criminal purpose. Your Honours, those are my submissions relating to how the link is made. I hope I have managed to address Your Honours' concerns in your question. Of course, I expect Your Honours' questions following if there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: There are no specific questions. You have addressed the question we put, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'd like to address two distinct issues. First, a clarification with regard to Martic's conviction for detention crimes in the Benkovac area; and then I'd like to respond to the third question posed by the Chamber in the order for preparation of the appeals hearing. I don't intend to present any argument on grounds 1 to 4 or 9 and 10 of the Defence appeal; however, I am available for any questions that you might have. I'd like to begin by clarifying the Prosecution's position concerning Martic's conviction for detention crimes in the Benkovac area, which we submit should be reversed for reasons of fairness. We've advised the appellant's counsel of this just prior to the hearing. In the judgement, the Trial Chamber convicts Martic of torture as a violation of the laws or customs of war for two victims at the Benkovac SJB; and for inhumane acts and cruel treatment of three victims at a nearby location in Biljani. And I'd refer you to the Trial Chamber's factual findings at paragraphs 227 and 228 of the judgement and legal findings at paragraphs 422 and 424 and also reference to 477 regarding the cumulative convictions. Martic has challenged the reasonableness of these findings at paragraph 197 of his appeal brief, and the Prosecution has responded at paragraphs 141 and 142 of our respondent's brief. The Prosecution acknowledges that these convictions should be reversed for reasons of fairness. These charges did not form part of the case against the accused; Benkovac was not one of the detention sites listed in the indictment; and the Prosecution did not seek a conviction for these incidents. To be very specific, this would affect the Trial Chamber's legal findings concerning Milan Martic's criminal responsibility for crimes committed against persons in detention in the Benkovac area as set out in paragraphs 422 and 424 of the trial judgement. Your Honours, this concession should not have any impact on Martic's sentence. The Benkovac incidents involved a total of five victims and formed a small part of the underlying crime-base supporting Martic's convictions for crimes committed against detainees in Counts 7, 8, and 9. The crime-base underpinning these three counts also includes Martic's criminal responsibility for crimes committed at three other detention facilities: The JNA 9th Corps barracks in Knin, the old hospital in Knin, and the Titovo Korenica SJB where hundreds of non-Serbs were illegally detained, many of whom were subjected to torture, cruel treatment, and other inhumane acts. Your Honours, unless you have any questions on that issue, I will turn to question 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can go to question 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: In order to answer question 3, it's important to first address what Martic means when he claims to have promoted co-existence. What he means is not co-existence in the ordinary sense; he means separate existence in ethnically divided territories. For example, in the Thornberry meeting minutes, which is Exhibit 965 at page 5, Martic is recorded as saying: "Joint life of Croats and Serbs in one state is impossible." He explains that: "I am convinced that we will be good neighbours as separate states." Martic also uses the term "co-existence" in the Kijevo ultimatum, which is Exhibit 212. He speaks of co-existence, but the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 443 that the threat expressed in Martic's ultimatum was carried out through the commission of widespread and grave crimes, which created an atmosphere of fear in which the further presence of Croats and other non-Serbs in these territories was made impossible. We can see from the totality of the evidence that what Martic really wanted was, in his own words from Exhibit 967, which is a letter dated 3 April 1993 signed by Milan Martic and others, what he wanted was "a state for all Serbs." It is the Prosecution's position that Martic promoted ethnic separation rather than co-existence by, as the Trial Chamber correctly found in paragraph 445, participating in a joint criminal enterprise to establish an ethnically Serb territory through the displacement of the Croat and other non-Serb population. This is clear from the Trial Chamber's findings throughout the judgement, but I would refer you in particular to paragraphs 337 to 342 concerning Martic's knowledge and reaction to the crimes that were being committed; paragraphs 447 to 455 concerning Martic's participation in the JCE to drive out the non-Serbs from the Krajina; and paragraph 295 to 301, including the evidence cited in footnote 917 regarding the facts of deportation including the role of the MUP and other groups used by the JCE. The Prosecution's position is borne out by the absence of concrete measures that Martic could be said to have taken to achieve inter-ethnic co-existence. Notably, none are cited in paragraph 203 of his brief, which forms the basis of your question. The Trial Chamber found at paragraph 498 that as one of the most important and influential political figures in the area, Martic was obligated to ensure that all inhabitants of his territory enjoyed respect for human rights. Had Martic really wanted to achieve co-existence in the sense of the different ethnicities sharing the Krajina, then there was much that he could have done to achieve this goal. For example, he could have used the police and the TO to secure the territory; he could have prevented and investigated the widespread crimes that were occurring; he could have taken harsh measures against the members of the police and the TO who were participating in these crimes. But this is not what we see from the judgement. Instead, the Trial Chamber found that Martic used his position, the police, and the TO to drive the non-Serbs from the area, and he protected those who were committing crimes. For example, he ordered the release of ten TO members who had been arrested by Captain Dragan for killing civilians. That's at paragraph 340 of the judgement. Martic actively advocated and pursued a goal of an ethnically Serb state, paragraph 341. Martic repeatedly and publicly opposed the return of the refugees, paragraph 4 -- sorry, 452. In concluding that Martic intended to forcibly displace the non-Serb population, the Trial Chamber gave detailed consideration to all of the evidence, including the few examples of what the Chamber ultimately characterizes as sporadic benevolent acts. Many of these were highlighted this afternoon. They were highlighted and isolated from the rest of the record. They were all considered by the Trial Chamber. In light of the totality of the evidence, the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that Martic deliberately refrained from intervening against perpetrators who committed crimes against the non-Serb population, again, paragraph 451; and that he intended the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, even where Martic took small steps that might be seen as supporting the non-Serbs, we can see from the judgement that other motives may have been at play. For example, Martic encouraged the equal treatment of non-Serb detainees. When asked why, Martic responded: "Because they have to be exchanged ..." and you can see that at footnote 1055. Martic disbanded Veljko Radunovic's police unit, but he did so mainly because they were trying to join Dubica to BiH, not because they had massacred 41 detainees or participated in other crimes in the region. Your Honours, your third question asks the Prosecution to elaborate on Martic's challenge to paragraph 452 of the trial judgement, where the Chamber finds that at a meeting on 14 June 1993 between Martic and Cedric Thornberry, the UNPROFOR director of civil affairs, Martic requested that: " ... Croats who wish to leave the RSK sign statements that nobody had put pressure on them to leave." In doing so, the Trial Chamber found that Martic was aware of the persecutorian course of atmosphere which existed and had existed in the SAO Krajina and RSK for some time and that those non-Serbs who expressed a desire to leave the territory did so without having a genuine choice in their displacement. In light of the Trial Chamber's other findings, the Trial Chamber was reasonable and correct to find that from 1991 onwards, and obviously also on the 14th of June, 1993, when he met with Thornberry, Martic was aware of the widespread forcible removal of the non-Serbs from the Krajina. The Trial Chamber made extensive findings concerning Martic's intent and his participation in the forcible displacement of the non-Serbs from the Krajina and his active participation in the joint criminal enterprise directed towards that goal. In summary, Your Honours, through the totality of his words and his deeds, Martic promoted ethnic separation and not co-existence. That concludes my submissions, unless you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't believe we have any.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Then that concludes the submissions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Then we'll turn to the Defence for their reply. You have 30 minutes for your reply, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend in his response says that we said long time ago and even the Trial Chamber said that creating ethnically pure territory by way of displacement of non-Serb population was the goal of the joint criminal enterprise, that the goal was to unify with Serbia and that that was achieved through attacks on Croat settlements and through the campaign of violence. In order for the Prosecution to state such an argument, I think they would need to support it by reference to specific evidence. The Prosecutor invoked Martic's statement concerning the Kijevo ultimatum, Exhibit 212, where allegedly it is stated that the co-existence with Croats was not possible; and Martic issued such an ultimatum in order to insist that the Croats remove the police station they had opened in Kijevo for no apparent reason. About the goal of the leadership of Krajina to unite with Serbia ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can continue, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. About the wish and the goal of the Krajina leadership to unite with Serbia, that alone is not sufficient proof of joint criminal enterprise. Are there any problems, Your Honours, or shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. So in our brief, we pointed out that the delegation of Krajina in April of 1991, when they travelled to Belgrade with their request to have Krajina join Serbia, they were not even allowed to enter the premises of the Assembly. Nobody saw them there. I pointed out the relevant statements of Mr. Kirudja, who confirmed that Mr. Milosevic had never had such an idea or a concept. And we pointed out the reason why Croatian -- why Krajina leadership had to oppose the Croatian policy, Exhibit 237, where Croats said that the issue of Knin would be resolved by slaughtering all of them. When the OTP spoke about the scope of joint criminal enterprise, they based their argument on Kijevo, again, which they treated as the first example of cooperation between the TO of Krajina and the JNA. The cooperation itself and activities, combat activities, are something that the OTP uses to prove the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution in doing so completely ignores the evidence admitted. Witness MM-114 on page 10665 and also on page 10666 clearly spoke about the reasons why the JNA attacked Kijevo; namely, the main roads were blocked, Croatian authorities set up a police station numbering 150 heavily armed policemen in Kijevo for no apparent reasons. These policemen abused the local Serbian population including the children, and the JNA action was not launched until they killed three members of the JNA while they were in the separation zone between the Croatian and the Serbian sides. Witness Borislav Djukic, General Djukic, who was in command of this operation gave identical explanations for this operation. Therefore, the cooperation between the JNA and Territorial Defence and the police cannot be used as evidence all by itself of the existence of joint criminal enterprise; neither can the Kijevo operation be used to support that claim. When discussing the role of the persons from paragraph 446 who allegedly were members of the joint criminal enterprise, my learned friend speaks about the cooperation between the JNA and the rebel Serbian population, Territorial Defence, and the police. That cooperation is not challenged, Your Honours, is not contentious. What my learned friend ignores is just a minor fact, namely, that in August 1991 the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a member of the United Nations; it was -- it had one single military power, which was the JNA and Territorial Defence, and that in accordance with the constitution then in force, both the JNA, the Territorial Defence, and all units resubordinated to them were under the command of the JNA. And the person in charge of the unit was responsible for their actions. That's issue number 1. Croatia did not exist in another continent. It was a federal unit of Yugoslavia, and the separatist leadership of Croatia attacked using their own forces both the JNA and the population. Exhibit 237 speaks clearly about that where they say Knin will disappear as such; we will take Knin by way of arms. President Tudjman clearly says that the Serbian issue in Croatia has been resolved; there will be no more than 3 per cent of them living in Croatia. Your Honours, in assessing the reason why they acted under those circumstances, why the JNA acted together with the Territorial Defence, police, and everybody else, one cannot ignore the international law; one cannot ignore the United Nations; one cannot ignore the then-existing world order. Yugoslavia at that time was one of the 45 member states who founded the UN, and this was taking place in the territory of the SFRY. Yugoslav government, be it complete or rump, was responsible for commanding the JNA, and the fact that these JNA units were under their command cannot be used as a fact that merely on its own supports the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. The OTP confirms that what I'm saying as true because the -- it is stated in documents that the units were resubordinated to the JNA. Well, naturally they were because that is how it was envisaged in the constitution. Everybody was resubordinated to the JNA units, but when it comes to Skabrnja, Nadin, and Saborsko, something else was taking place there. It was not an attack on undefended villages as the Prosecution claims. This campaign where the Martic's forces are attacking and the JNA is using artillery is something that exists only in the head of the witness called Milan Babic. The Trial Chamber quoted him in their judgement without asking for confirmation, and this witness is somebody whose credibility is seriously challenged. To accept him as a credible witness in light of the fact that this man killed himself is something that cannot be comprehended. This is unprecedented. The man who was obviously mentally seriously disturbed was accepted as a credible witness on essential issues. The OTP referred to the witness called Martic [sic] who had been sent from Serbia to Krajina, and this is yet another evidence that the Prosecution is not familiar with the Yugoslav constitution. The seat of all institutions, all federal institutions, was in Belgrade. The fact that Belgrade is also located in Serbia is something that the Prosecutor uses to support their thesis that since he had come from Serbia, that's yet another evidence of the existence of joint criminal enterprise. Maksic came to Krajina in order to establish Territorial Defence in Krajina. Territorial Defence was one of the components of the armed forces of Yugoslavia under the then-valid Yugoslav constitution. Speaking about Martic's role and cooperation with the persons listed in paragraph 446 -- well, we argued this extensively in our appeal. I wouldn't now want to repeat those arguments. What the Prosecutor is noting in particular is evidence of the existence of a common criminal purpose and joint criminal enterprise, that's the training camp in Golubic. I quoted from testimony of Witness Medakovic in my presentation, and he said that Krajina was surrounded. There was no electricity; there was no water; there was -- there were no medications; there was nothing. It was surrounded by Croat forces that were far stronger, the forces that planned to resolve the Serb issue by a massacre. We will slaughter Knin, as indicated in Exhibit 237. And when Mr. Martic as the chief of police in Golubic sets up a police training centre in Golubic, well, the Prosecution sees this as proof of existence of a common criminal purpose and a joint criminal enterprise. Well, what police force does not undergo training? Could you please tell me that, Your Honours. There is no police force in the world. And Witness Medakovic, I quoted the relevant page in the transcript, he showed what Martic's purpose was when he set up this training camp in Golubic. You can see that in the transcript today -- well, Medakovic says: I don't want any kind of cowboy vigilante police. I don't want to give weapons to people who had not undergone training. This is Martic's purpose, not what the Prosecution is saying. As regards Lovinac, that location is not listed in the indictment at all, so I don't know what the Prosecution is all about there. When my colleague from the Prosecution quotes General Mladic's words, let me remind you August and September 1991, that's the period when the regular armed forces of the state that still existed at the time of the Yugoslav state, and that was the Yugoslav People's Army and all those that were under its command, and the Prosecution spoke about the resubordination of units are duty-bound to comply with the orders of whoever is in command of the units. In our briefs and in our presentation today, we noted what the real reasons for the attacks on Kijevo, Skabrnja, Saborsko, Nadin were. Those were military fortifications set up by the Croatian authorities in the Serb ethnic territory, and the purpose was to cut off roads, to attack the JNA, to maltreat and kill the population. Those were regular, legitimate military actions. The fact that the milicija, the police, and the TO participated in those operations cannot be held as evidence of the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. When we're talking about Kostajnica -- well, I really can't understand the position taken by my learned friend from the Prosecution. The fighting for Kostajnica ended on the 12th or 13th of September, 1991. That is not contentious. We showed evidence that the local population participated in the fighting, 5 to 600 people, including 117 Croats who were members of the Territorial Defence, local Territorial Defence, so I don't know what evidence the Prosecution used to place the JNA and Martic's police in this force. There is no such evidence on the record, but what is interesting is the link established between the previous fighting in Kostajnica in September 1991. This is when Tudjman ordered the evacuation of Serbs and of -- the local Croat population and the ZNG units from the area of Dubica, Bacin, and Kostajnica, and the crimes that were committed in October, on the 20th of October, by groups bent on revenge. That is impermissible, and it is not borne out by facts. We noted that in our appeal, so I'm just briefly referring to that here in my oral arguments. Of courses the victims in Cerovljani, Bacin, and Dubica, they are innocent victims, people who died, who were killed, but you can find such victims in every war. What is really terrible here is that the Prosecution says that those people were killed either by the TO, the JNA, or the police or paramilitaries, so we don't know who it was, but at any rate Mr. Martic's responsible for it. Why? Well, because he's alive; he's there. I can't see any other reason, Your Honours. We don't know who committed the crimes, and my learned friend confirms that when he provides a clarification as to how this alleged leadership of the JCE actually did its work. They used members of the JNA, of the TO, of milicija, the police, and paramilitaries, and God knows who else who may have been unwilling or unwitting tools, but those who organized them, they knew what they were all about. So the Prosecution in this case was not even interested in identifying the actual perpetrators. It doesn't know who the actual perpetrators are, but still they're there to claim that Mr. Martic is responsible despite all the evidence that has come in, and we pointed you to some of the evidence that might indicate who it is. Is it possible that the political goals of the Serbs in Krajina or the political leadership of Yugoslavia or of the JNA, to discuss this -- those goals without knowing what the goals of Croatia were in the same area at the same time. And we called evidence as to their goals and as to their actions. I spoke about that today. I will take this opportunity with apologies to the Appeals Chamber to quote what a witness said before this Tribunal yesterday or the day before yesterday. Because I was preparing for this hearing, I was unable to follow this in detail. I'm talking about the evidence by US Ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith, about Operation Storm where he says that President Tudjman wanted to create a Greater Croatia, and some of his interlocutors were happy with a smaller Greater Croatia, but at any rate this state was not to include any Serbs, and that was in the Gotovina case, and I think that you should actually admit this transcript into evidence here because I think that would be really interesting and important for the findings of fact in this case. When he talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, are you wishing to introduce new evidence? But it's a stage in which it's -- should ask for leave to do that, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honour, I'm merely saying this to illustrate the point, as a suggestion to the Appeals Chamber, that it might consider ex officio because of the importance of the issues that are on the agenda, the issue of a joint criminal enterprise, and it is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that the Chambers should do that proprio motu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You were saying you wanted to bring something that would be interesting and important for the findings of fact in this case. So you are trying to bring in new evidence at this stage, I think? It's not just a mere consideration you're making. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, formally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't see how you could do that at this point, I mean, at this stage of the appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not want to tender anything into evidence. I'm talking about this transcript. That was not my intention. I used it merely to illustrate a point, something that this Tribunal should be aware of, something that might be of bearing for this case. So if you allow me, I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, I may ask the Prosecutor their reaction to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, and Your Honours, I would like to state the Prosecution's position that this is not an appropriate procedure, not only just at this juncture of the appeals proceedings, but certainly it is not appropriate to simply refer to evidence that is not on the record before this Chamber from another case, and we object to the Defence attempts to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. The objection is accepted by the Chamber. So please continue but not on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've explained that I didn't actually want to tender this into evidence as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please don't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about the events regarding Dubica, Cerovljani, and Bacin, my colleagues from the Prosecution, not only are they trying to shift the suffering of the civilian population in the hands of various renegade groups one month earlier; they happened one month later, and today they mentioned some places that are not in the indictment. We were forced to look at two maps. What bearing has anything that happened anywhere else in Croatia on what was happening in the locations listed in the indictment? That's completely unacceptable. Now, whether this location Predore is 8 or 88 kilometres away from Dubica, that's completely irrelevant. The fact that the JNA and the Territorial Defence were operating there and the entire territory of Croatia was affected by heavy fighting at that time, well, this location in Krajina is not the only place where fighting was going on at that time. The UN forces were deployed there because the fiercest fighting was in the Krajina area. So Predore cannot be used as -- to support any arguments about the presence of the JNA and the TO in the Dubica area at the time and least of all to support claims about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. And perhaps what the Prosecution said about the events in Dubica shows what the standard of proof is for the Prosecution and what was accepted by the Trial Chamber. The fact that the local TO staff of the Serb forces was set up in Dubica on the 14th or on the 15th of September, it is reasonable to conclude that the Serb forces were responsible. Your Honours, the fact that it is reasonable to conclude this, that is quite far removed from evidence beyond any doubt, and we presented evidence beyond any doubt that people who were in direct conflict with Martic, local Chetniks, were responsible for the crimes in Dubica, and that's what I said today, and the same goes for Bacin. Again, the Prosecution involves the TO, the JNA, and the police in those activities there. I personally am of belief that although the Prosecution is there to prosecute, because it is part of the Tribunal in accordance with the Statute it also has the same task as the rest of the Tribunal, which is part of the Tribunal's mandate to find truth. This is what Judge Schomburg was talking about. When we're talking about Saborsko, well, we've presented all our arguments, and Witness Medakovic explained that after the Saborsko operation there was a unit that was tasked with securing the combat zone that the JNA units had left; and in any society, in any unit, there is scum, thugs, who can kill, torch, plunder, but the character of the operations, the TG 2 war diary, Exhibit 108 and Exhibit 52, order for the Saborsko operations, shows that the fighting had different character. It's an order to fight and beat the opposing -- the enemy armed forces and the axes of advance are clearly stated, the locations where the enemy forces are deployed are clearly designated. And I forgot to mention when I was talking about Kijevo. My learned friends from the Prosecution seem to forget the fact that nobody was killed in the operation in Kijevo, that 60 police officers were captured, ethnic Croats wearing uniforms, and that Martic did issue this order that was quoted by the Prosecution. Don't let anything happen to these people; don't let any of them get hurt or killed. That's what he said when he went there to control this whole thing, but this is taken by the Prosecution as evidence of the criminal purpose. The Prosecution explains their vision -- their interpretation of the term co-existence, as Martic used it, and they explained that Martic did not want this co-existence to take place in a single state. He thought that this was impossible, yet we presented arguments to the effect that the Croatian authorities had made it impossible for Croats and Serbs to live in the same state because of their plan to resolve the Serbian issue through massacre, and Tudjman himself said that he was happy his wife was not Serb or Jewish and that he was happy - that's what he said in 1996 - that the Serb question in Croatia was resolved and that there would never again be more than 3 per cent of Serbs living in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Counsel, may I ask you to conclude because it's already half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. I'm about to wrap up. I have one minute, and I will bear in mind your warning. In essence, the Prosecution position about Mr. Martic's responsibility relies on the failure to distinguish between the obligation of conduct and obligation of result, and the Prosecution believes that what the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 498 is correct, that the -- that Mr. Martic had to ensure respect of human rights for everybody, and that's what the Trial Chamber says about the territory in state of war, state of armed conflict, and that's one of the first preconditions for the jurisdiction of this Tribunal: There has to be armed conflict. And now Mr. Martic is under an obligation to protect everyone, to prevent any crimes. And the Trial Chamber fails to prove or to show how this area protected by the UN could be massacred by Croats for four years, and the United Nations were unable to protect the Serb population in Operations Maslenica, Medak, and so on. And Cedric Thornberry said to Martic, my UN civilian police chief explained to me and told me that you, Mr. Martic, are doing a great job protecting the Serb population in very difficult -- protecting the whole population in very difficult conditions. And that concludes my remarks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. This concludes the consideration of the appeal by Milan Martic. The Appeals Chamber will consider tomorrow, 9.00, the appeal by the Prosecution, but before adjourning let me raise one issue. In the Scheduling Order that was issued on the 15th of May, the Appeals Chamber cancelled a Status Conference that had been scheduled for the 27th of June, and that was because the hearing was convened for today. However, in light of this perhaps we could now ask -- I would like to ask Mr. Martic if he has any issue concerning limited to his detention to raise, he can do it now. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] As for the conditions of my detention and my health, I have nothing to discuss. Thank God, I'm fine. But as for tomorrow, I will have certain issues to raise within the ten minutes you allotted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So tomorrow you will have the time as foreseen in the Scheduling Order. So if there is no issue to be raised concerning your condition of detention, we can now adjourn for today, and the hearing will continue tomorrow at 9.00. Well, and the Status Conference remains cancelled, of course. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
